gamemechanicinfo-fornax-text:
Updraft Kiln

An updraft kiln fires far more pottery in one go than a pit kiln, burns much less fuel doing it, and needs no iron at all - so it can be built long before a beehive kiln (which needs a kiln door, and iron) is within reach. It is a chimney of raw mud brick: the fire below, the wares in the middle, and a draft vent at the top that pulls the heat up through them. Where a pit kiln burns two firewood per ware, this burns closer to a quarter of one.

Building it
Place the firebox where you want the front of the kiln to be - it turns to face you as you place it, and the rest of the kiln runs away behind it. Then Ctrl + rightmouse click the firebox with an empty hand: a blueprint of ghost blocks appears showing every block still to place, and the same click takes it down again. Green is mud brick, blue-grey is a grate tile, blue is a mud seal, and red means something is in the way that needs clearing.

The kiln is a 5x5 drum around a 3x3x4 chamber, four courses tall, that then steps in to a 3x3 chimney neck and cap. The four corners of the drum stop at grate level - the two courses above them are left open, which is what gives the kiln its shape, though nothing stops you filling them back in or leaning something against them. Walls may be mudbrick or cob, in any mix.

The ground course is a ring of wall with the firebox set into the middle of the front and a single mud brick pillar standing in the centre of the chamber. On top of that pillar go nine kiln grate tiles, which form the floor the wares sit on. Grate tiles are clay-formed and then fired in a pit kiln, so you must use the older technology once to build the newer one. Above the grate are two courses of ware chamber and flue, whose front three blocks are the loading entrance, and above those the neck and the draft vent at the very top.

Firing
Set green pottery or raw bricks on the grate as ordinary ground storage - around thirty pieces of small pottery, or two hundred raw bricks. Close the loading entrance with six mud seals, put fuel in the firebox, and light it with a firestarter or a lit torch. Once it is burning the firebox is sealed: fuel can be neither added nor taken out until the batch is done, so load it fully before lighting it.

A batch takes a fixed amount of fuel energy whatever you burn - hotter fuel simply gets through it faster. Thirty firewood will fire a full load in about thirteen hours, twenty-nine peat bricks in about eight, and eighteen charcoal in about six. Anything burning cooler than 650 degrees is refused. Look at the firebox at any time and it will tell you how many hours of burn are loaded, and say so if that is not enough to see the batch out.

What it fires
Pottery and raw bricks come out as the same colours a pit kiln would give them - this kiln changes how many you can fire at once and how little fuel it takes, not what you get. The colour range a beehive kiln offers, which it varies by how many of its doors it leaves open, stays a beehive kiln's to give.

It is not only pottery. Crushed lime fires here too, two lime to one quicklime, twelve to a pile and nine piles to a grate - a lime kiln is an updraft shaft kiln, which is exactly what this is. Anything a mod has marked as kiln work is accepted as well; anything the kiln cannot fire, it will say so rather than sit there burning firewood over it.

The firebox shows its state from across the yard: dark when empty, firewood in the mouth when fuelled and waiting, glowing red coals while the chamber warms, and bright orange flame once it is up to temperature.

Opening it early
Breaking a seal - or any part of the shell - while the kiln is hot lets cold air in, and thermal shock will shatter a share of the load. The chance climbs from nothing at 450 degrees to about half the batch at full heat, which is exactly when the firebox turns from red to orange: once it looks like it is firing, it has become expensive to open. Below that everything survives, so an early change of mind costs nothing. Whatever survives keeps the heat it has already taken, so a repaired kiln picks up where it left off.

Running out of fuel
If the firebox empties before the batch is done the kiln simply goes out. The seals stay whole, the wares stay green, and the hours of heat already put in are kept - top the firebox up, light it again, and the same batch carries on. What you cannot do is leave it. Most of what a firing costs is the climb to temperature, so once the chamber has fallen back to ambient a share of that progress is gone and has to be burned again. Relighting a kiln that is still warm costs nothing at all.

The mud seals crack in every firing and must be replaced for the next one - six per batch, at four clay and a block of dirt each. That is twenty-four clay and six dirt every firing, and it is the kiln's real running cost - what it saves you in firewood it asks for in clay. The shell itself lasts indefinitely.
